blocks.text: 80s-90s Afrocentrism was a design style, fashion trend, and cultural movement that occurred in the 1980s and 1990s and existed until its decline in the early 2000s. This aesthetic was apart of the Pan Africanism and Afrocentric movements, promoting racial unity across the global Black diaspora and giving African people agency over their own history through disproving and correcting Eurocentric biases in philosophy, history, and education. This aesthetic is characterized by the usage of African prints and patterns, the Pan-African colors (green, yellow, black, and red), and the centering of Black people, cultures, and stories in popular media.

Throughout the 1970s and '80s, several countries within Africa fought for and gained freedom from their colonizing powers: Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Angola, and Djibouti in the 70s, Zimbabwe in 1980, and Namibia in 1990. 1990 also saw the end of apartheid in South Africa, and Nelson Mandela became president of South Africa in 1994. This 30-year period was an era of fresh Black positivity and hope all over the diaspora, with Afrocentrism in particular gaining the most traction in the 80s and 90s.

This positive mindset was reflected in popular media, with a rise in diversity and representation in television and film. Aided by the Black demographic newly gaining economic power and the rise of Hip-Hop, the world began to see Black stories being told with a depth and respect that they hadn't prior. Black-led sitcoms like The Cosby Show, A Different World, Martin and Living Single put Black culture and narratives front-and-center in the American eye. The 80s-90s Afrocentrism aesthetic was a direct result of these things: a mixture of African political power, an Afrocentric reclamation of Black history, and a cultural shift in America towards the acceptance and portrayal of Black lives in media. These things enabled this aesthetic to arise and thrive, allowing the Black community to have pride in their ethnicities and roots out loud, without social criticism.

This period of Afrocentrism also saw the rise of Kwanzaa as a holiday, which became widely adopted and commercialized alongside the broader Afrocentric cultural movement happening at the time. Much of the visual media of the era included Kwanzaa as a Black-focused alternative to Christmas, and educated the masses on its existence and practices. Rugrats, The Proud Family, and even Arthur had Kwanzaa-centric episodes air during the tail end of the 80s-90s Afrocentrism aesthetic boom, in 2000 and 2001.
The color palette of 80s-90s Afrocentrism is primarily taken from the colors of the two flags that represent Pan-Africanism: the flag of Ethiopia and the Black Liberation flag.

For the former, the colors represent development (green), hope (yellow) and the blood of Ethiopians spilled in defense from colonialism (red). These colors are common to many African national flags, borrowed from the flag of Ethiopia out of respect for their defeat of colonizing powers.

For the latter, the colors represent the "the blood that unites all people of Black African ancestry, and shed for liberation" (red), "Black people whose existence as a nation is affirmed by the existence of the flag" (black), and "the abundant natural wealth of Africa" (green) as per the Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League. In addition to green, yellow, red, and black, orange and purple are also utilizied, with orange specifically becoming associated with the Black community through the 2000s due to its usage in ethnic haircare marketing and advertising. Purple also gained significance within the Black community through several cultural staples centering the color, such as the 1982 book The Color Purple, the Prince album Purple Rain in 1984, and the Jimi Hendrix song "Purple Haze" of 1967, as well as due to its pre-existing associations with royalty.

African and geometric prints are prevalent visuals of the aesthetic (triangles, lines, zigzags, dots and circles, waves, spirals), as are petroglyphs and glyph-reminiscent figures, and visual representations of the continent of Africa.

80s-90s Afrocentrism prioritized Black-owned brands and African garments. Dashiki shirts, headwraps and kufi hats began to emerge in popular culture, and the usage of African prints and Pan African colors became popular alongside them. Afrocentric brands like Premier International and Cross Colours debuted during this time, as well as several Black-owned brands like FUBU and Karl Kani. Clothing with graphics of prominent Black political figures (like Malcolm X and MLK Jr.) and clothing repping HBCUs were also common. Gold jewelry was often worn to compliment the colors of the fashion and as a tie to African culture. Bomber jackets were popular, as were both sunglasses and fashion glasses. This aesthetic also saw Black women beginning to embrace their natural hair and protective styles, with box braids, locs, and hair decorations like beads rising in popularity both in real life and in fiction through film and television.
